analysis.one_liner: Sets binding standards for immigration detention, ends private detention contracts, and ends mandatory detention.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 158 House members, never received a committee vote or floor action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Department of Homeland Security to write enforceable standards for every facility holding immigration detainees, based on American Bar Association standards. It would order unannounced inspections by the department's Inspector General, with fines or contract termination for facilities that fail, public reporting of deaths in custody within 24 hours, and disclosure of facility contracts under the Freedom of Information Act. It would phase out all contracts with private companies and local jails for immigration detention within three years, ban the detention of children, and replace mandatory detention with a hearing before an immigration judge where release is the default presumption.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 50,000 people held in immigration detention on a given day, their families, and people seeking asylum who today can be held without a bond hearing. It also benefits workers who could no longer be detained as retaliation for filing wage or workplace complaints, and taxpayers if government-run or lower-cost community supervision replaces paid private beds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Immigration detainees, asylum seekers, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Requires DHS detention standards to meet at least the American Bar Association's Civil Immigration Detention Standards, with biennial updates [S3].

Requires at least annual unannounced Inspector General inspections, public release of inspection reports within 60 days, and escalating penalties for failing facilities: a fine of at least 10% of the contract value on a first failure, and transfer of detainees plus contract termination on a second failure within two years [S3].

Requires notification to Congress within 24 hours of any death in DHS custody and a public investigation report, including a root-cause analysis led by a qualified medical professional, within 60 days [S3].

Makes inspection reports and detention facility contracts public records under the Freedom of Information Act, and requires monthly public posting of facility-level data including bed counts, average detention stays, and compliance status [S3].

Bars any new or extended contracts with outside operators of secure detention facilities and requires termination of existing contracts within three years, after which all facilities must be owned and operated by DHS [S3].
Prohibits detaining anyone under 18 in a facility operated or contracted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and states that detention of children inflicts severe, irreparable harm [S3].

Repeals mandatory detention for asylum seekers: immigrants would get a custody hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours, release would be presumed unless DHS proves with clear and convincing evidence that the person is a flight risk or danger, and conditions must be the least restrictive necessary [S3].

Requires bond amounts be set based on the person's ability to pay, protects vulnerable people and primary caregivers from detention unless community supervision is impracticable, and bans charging detainees more than the cost of operating an ankle monitor [S3].
Creates a private right of action letting a detained person injured by a standards violation sue in federal court for injunctive relief and damages, with attorney fees for the prevailing party [S3].

Protects people who file workplace claims: a person who has filed a wage, labor, or civil rights claim counts as a vulnerable person who generally may not be detained, which removes the threat of detention as leverage against workers asserting labor rights [S3].
Requires an updated online detainee locator within 12 hours of any custody change, so families can find detained relatives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies and county and local jails that hold ICE detainees under contract would lose that revenue within three years, and for-profit electronic monitoring providers could no longer charge immigrants above-cost fees for ankle monitors. DHS would take on the cost of standing up its own facilities and of funding nonprofit community-based supervision programs. Enforcement opponents also argue ending mandatory detention and setting a low default for release would let more people facing removal remain free while their cases proceed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison firms, county jails, and for-profit monitor vendors

drawbacks.text: The phase-out requires DHS to replace roughly the entire current detention bed network — largely private contractors and county jails — with government-owned facilities within three years, an enormous construction, staffing, and siting task that could exceed the timeline and cost more in the short run [S3].

The bill abolishes mandatory detention categories, including for asylum seekers at the border, and makes release the presumptive default that DHS must rebut with clear and convincing evidence; opponents of immigration enforcement argue this would substantially reduce detention of people subject to removal [S3].
Ending the use of local jails could shrink detention capacity in remote areas near the border, potentially lengthening transfers and straining the court system's ability to hear cases quickly [S3].
The civil cause of action against facilities that violate standards could generate significant litigation against DHS and its operators, and attorney-fee awards add taxpayer exposure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in immigration detention, the benefits are direct and large: enforceable standards, independent inspections, public accountability for deaths, a judge instead of automatic detention, and no child detention. The real drawbacks are execution risk — rebuilding the detention system as government-owned within three years is a heavy lift — and a policy shift that opponents consider a de facto loosening of immigration enforcement. The bill is a broad restructuring rather than a narrow oversight fix, and its success would depend on funding and implementation not addressed in the text.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees and then to two subcommittees, and neither committee ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021 without any vote.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill in the House on April 30, 2019, joined by Representative Adam Smith of Washington [S1].
157 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, in addition to the sponsor [S4].
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and the Homeland Security Committee on the day of introduction, and the Speaker split referral between the committees [S5].
On May 7 it was referred to the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Border Security, Facilitation, and Operations, and on May 20 to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration and Citizenship [S5].
No hearing, markup, vote, or floor action ever followed; the last action of record was the subcommittee referral in May 2019, and the bill died at the end of the 116th Congress in January 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison companies and county jails kept their ICE detention contracts, and DHS retained its discretion over detention standards, inspections, and who it holds, without the independent inspections, public death reporting, and contract disclosure the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison contractors and ICE's own discretion

sides.party_line_note: All 158 supporters for whom the record identifies a party were Democrats, including the sponsor and 157 cosponsors; no Republican cosponsor is listed, and no Republican is recorded as speaking or acting for the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Private prison and detention facility contractors
industries.note: The bill bars any new contract with outside operators and terminates existing contracts within three years, after which all detention facilities must be owned and run by DHS. These companies hold most ICE detention beds, so the bill would end their core federal revenue stream; the bill's failure left their contracts in place [S3].

industries.industry: County and local jails holding ICE detainees
industries.note: The phase-out covers agreements with any public or private entity operating a detention facility, so county jails that fill beds for ICE would lose that business. Jails could also face fines and contract termination for failing the new standards [S3].

The bill expands alternatives-to-detention programs, which could mean more monitoring contracts, but bars charging detainees any fee above the actual cost of operating an ankle monitor — a practice where vendors bill immigrants directly [S3].

DHS could contract with nongovernmental community organizations for case management and appearance-assistance programs as alternatives to detention, and non-secure programs must be run by nonprofits or DHS after the phase-out [S3].
